evidence.intree_statement: Definition Complete {C : Category} := ∀ (D : Category) (F : D ⟶ C), Limit F.
Definition Cocomplete {C : Category} := ∀ (D : Category) (F : D ⟶ C), Colimit F.

statement_record.book: A diagram is small when its indexing category is small. C is complete when it admits limits of all small diagrams valued in C, and cocomplete when it admits colimits of all small diagrams valued in C.
statement_record.intree: Definition Complete {C : Category} := ∀ (D : Category) (F : D ⟶ C), Limit F.  /  Definition Cocomplete {C : Category} := ∀ (D : Category) (F : D ⟶ C), Colimit F.
statement_record.strength_comparison: same. Both are Type-valued limit oracles (a function assigning a chosen Limit/Colimit to every diagram), matching the book's 'admits limits of all small diagrams'. The one presentational difference is the smallness discipline: there is no in-tree `Small` predicate on categories to define 'small diagram' with, so the quantification is over every `Category D` and the size restriction is carried by universe polymorphism — instantiating `Complete` constrains D's object/hom universes relative to C's (stated in the file header, Structure/Complete.v:29-37, and observed concretely at Adjunction/SAFT.v:138, where `Complete` forces the diagram category's hom universe to coincide with C's). So the in-tree reading is 'has a limit for every suitably small diagram', not the inconsistent all-diagrams reading.

statement_record.book: Example 3.2.5: by Theorem 3.2.4 the product of sets A_j indexed by a set J is the set of cones with summit * over the discrete J-indexed diagram, and such a cone is just a J-tuple; hence the categorical product in Set is the usual cartesian product ∏_{j∈J} A_j = {(a_j ∈ A_j)_{j∈J}}.
statement_record.intree: The categorical product of two setoids is the product setoid — carrier the product type, ≈ componentwise, projections fst/snd, pairing x ↦ (f x, g x) — and Cartesian_Limit identifies binary products with limits of discrete two-object diagrams.
statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-weaker: binary (J = 2) only. The underlying-set claim is exact for that case — the carrier IS the cartesian product type — but the arbitrary index set J of the book is not covered.

evidence.intree_statement: #[export] Program Instance FinSet_Pullbacks : HasPullbacks FinSet := { pullback := fun m n k (f : Fin.t m → Fin.t k) (g : Fin.t n → Fin.t k) => {| Pull := fin_countP (finset_pb_pred f g); pullback_fst := fun q => fst (fin_unpair (fin_select (finset_pb_pred f g) q)); pullback_snd := fun q => snd (fin_unpair (fin_select (finset_pb_pred f g) q)) |} }  where  finset_pb_pred f g := fun p => fin_eqb (f (fst (fin_unpair p))) (g (snd (fin_unpair p)))

Record Pullback {C : Category} {x y z : C} (f : x ~> z) (g : y ~> z) := { Pull : C; pullback_fst : Pull ~> x; pullback_snd : Pull ~> y; pullback_commutes : f ∘ pullback_fst ≈ g ∘ pullback_snd; ump_pullbacks : ∀ Q (q1 : Q ~> x) (q2 : Q ~> y), f ∘ q1 ≈ g ∘ q2 → ∃! u : Q ~> Pull, pullback_fst ∘ u ≈ q1 ∧ pullback_snd ∘ u ≈ q2 }

statement_record.book: Example 3.2.9: elements of the pullback of B →f A ←g C are cones with summit *, i.e. commutative squares, whose data is a pair (b,c) with f(b) = g(c); hence B ×_A C = {(b,c) ∈ B × C | f(b) = g(c)}. The following prose observes that this exhibits the pullback as the equalizer of f∘π_B, g∘π_C : B × C ⇉ A.
statement_record.intree: For the skeletal finite-set category FinSet, the pullback object is the counted subset of the encoded pairs Fin.t (m*n) satisfying `fin_eqb (f (fst (fin_unpair p))) (g (snd (fin_unpair p)))`, with projections decode-then-project and the full UMP discharged via rank/select.

statement_record.book: Example 3.2.14: an idempotent e : A → A (e∘e = e) has as its limit in Set the fixed-point set A^e = {a | ea = a}; equivalently A^e is the equalizer of id_A, e : A ⇉ A via s : A^e ↣ A. Since e is a cone over that pair, e = s r for a unique r, which SPLITS the idempotent, and s r s = e s = s with uniqueness gives r s = id_{A^e}, so A^e is a retract of A. Conversely any retract B →s A →r B with r s = id_B gives an idempotent s r split by B, and B ↣ A ⇉ A is an equalizer diagram.
statement_record.intree: In Sets the fixed-point sub-setoid `sets_split_obj e := {| carrier := ∃ a : X, e a ≈ a |}` carries a `SplitIdempotent Sets X (sets_split_obj e)` whose split_idem is e itself, with the two laws `split_idem_s ∘ split_idem_r ≈ e` and `split_idem_r ∘ split_idem_s ≈ id`; `Sets_IdempotentsSplit : IdempotentsSplit Sets` (line 101) says every idempotent of Sets splits this way.

statement_record.book: Exercise 3.2.i: redefine a small category as a diagram in Set — sets ob C and mor C with dom, cod : mor C → ob C and id : ob C → mor C, composition defined on the set of composable pairs obtained as a PULLBACK, with the category axioms expressed as commutative diagrams in Set; replacing Set by any category E with pullbacks defines a category internal to E.
statement_record.intree: `Record Metacategory` presents a category as set-level data — a set of arrows (arrow := N) together with an FMap `pairs` of composable pairs and their composites — with matchability, associativity and identity stated as first-order conditions on the `composite` relation; `object`/`morphism` recover the two sorts (objects are the identity arrows, a morphism carries dom/cod witnesses), and `Category_from_Metacategory : Category` proves such data yields a category.
statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-weaker on three counts: (i) the presentation is single-sorted (arrows-only, Mac Lane I.1) rather than the two-sorted ob/mor diagram the exercise asks for — dom and cod are not functions mor C → ob C but proof-carrying fields on `morphism`; (ii) the set of composable pairs is an FMap over `arrow := N`, so only categories whose arrows are indexed by numerals are expressible (the four in-tree examples are Zero/One/Two/Three/Four), and it is NOT obtained as a pullback; (iii) the axioms are first-order relational conditions, not commutative diagrams in Set.

gap: Two things the exercise asks for are entirely absent. (b) The generalization: there is no `InternalCategory` class, no 'category internal to E' for a category E with pullbacks — `internal` in-tree means only internal monoids/comonoids in a monoidal category (Theory/Algebra/Monoid.v, Theory/Algebra/Comonoid.v) and internal adjunctions in a bicategory.
